Females of the golden eye jobfish, Pristipomoides flavipinnis, attain a maximum recorded total length of 76.6 centimeters [Li = 76.6 centimeters], a size that places this lutjanid among the larger members of the deepwater snapper assemblage. This ultimate length was derived from an extensive sampling program targeting commercially exploited populations along the insular slopes of the tropical Pacific. Complementary growth reconstructions, based on otolith increment analyses from a regionally representative dataset, yielded a length-mass relationship that allowed the estimation of the corresponding wet weight. The calculated asymptotic body mass for females is 5351 grams [Wwi = 5351 grams], a figure consistent with the robust, laterally compressed body plan characteristic of bentho-pelagic predators occupying mesophotic reef habitats. This remarkable size is attained only after many years of steady somatic expansion, reflecting the relatively slow growth trajectory that defines this species within its genus.

The onset of reproductive maturity in female golden eye jobfish is signaled by the attainment of a total length of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters], a value determined through histological examination of gonadal tissues from specimens collected across seasonal sampling events. At this pubertal length, the corresponding wet weight is approximately 730 grams [Wwp = approximately 730 grams], as derived from the same length-weight conversion used for the adult population. The maturation schedule appears to be tightly linked to environmental temperature, with all laboratory-based developmental studies conducted at a stable thermal regime of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C]. This temperature reflects the ambient conditions found at the depths typically inhabited by this species on the outer reef slopes and seamounts of its range.

Early life history begins with the hatching of a small, pelagic egg. At the moment of eclosion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a wet weight of just 0.00029 grams [Wwb = 0.00029 grams], a value that is based on the geometric volume of an egg measuring 0.82 millimeters in diameter. The yolk-dependent prolarva then enters a critical endotrophic phase, relying entirely on its endogenous reserves. The duration of this pre-feeding stage is short; at the prevailing temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C], the age at hatching is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days]. This rapid early development is characteristic of tropical lutjanids and is likely an adaptation to reduce the window of vulnerability to planktonic predators. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs soon after the yolk sac is fully resorbed.

Reproductive output in Pristipomoides flavipinnis is considerable, reflecting the high fecundity typical of batch-spawning, iteroparous teleosts. Field studies conducted at the species' ambient thermal environment of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C] revealed that a single, large female can produce in excess of 950,000 eggs annually [Ri = 950,000 eggs annually]. This annual fecundity value is derived by scaling the reproductive rate of a closely related species, Lutjanus carponotatus, to account for differences in body size. Such a high output is an indication of a reproductive strategy that relies on the production of numerous, small pelagic eggs to maximize the probability of offspring recruitment into suitable habitats. This finding aligns with the general life-history pattern observed in deepwater snappers.

Longevity data for the golden eye jobfish indicate that this species possesses a comparatively extended lifespan for a tropical reef fish. The maximum documented lifespan under natural conditions, again measured at a stable temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C], is 40 years [am = 40 years]. This remarkable longevity, equivalent to over fourteen thousand days, is a key component of its slow life-history strategy, allowing for repeated reproductive events across many spawning seasons. Such a long adult phase, coupled with the delayed maturation and high asymptotic mass, positions P. flavipinnis as a species with relatively low natural mortality and a demographic profile that is particularly sensitive to over-exploitation by deepwater fisheries. The combination of these life-history traits underscores the need for cautious management of this valuable stock.
